'''Donald R. Hamann''' (born 1939) is an American [[physicist]].

== Early life and education ==
Donald R. Hamann pursued his higher education at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he completed his Ph.D. in physics in 1965.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MIT Institute Archives & Special Collections. Massachusetts Institute of Technology. News Office (AC0069) |url=https://cdn.libraries.mit.edu/dissemination/diponline/AC0069_NewReleases/NewsRelease_1960/AC0069_1961/AC0069_196106_028.pdf |website=MIT}}</ref>

== Career and Research ==
Hamann began his professional career at [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]] in [[Murray Hill, New Jersey]], where he worked from 1965 until 2001.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hamann, Donald, 1939- |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11507011.html |access-date=2024-10-07 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref>

In 2001, he joined [[Rutgers University]] as a visiting scientist in the Department of Physics and Astronomy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Donald R. Hamann |url=https://cgisvr.physics.rutgers.edu/cgi-bin/physdb/genpip.pl?Hamann |access-date=2024-10-07 |website=cgisvr.physics.rutgers.edu}}</ref>

== Awards and recognition ==
In 1979, he was awarded the [[Davisson–Germer Prize|Davisson-Germer Prize]] in Atomic or Surface Physics by the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honors and Award Winners |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/winners?award_recipients%5Bpage%5D=1227 |website=aps.org}}</ref>
